newsitem.title: USA: Tennessee budget seen tightening more in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Tennessee budget seen tightening more in 1998.

text.p: Tennessee's new $14.5 billion budget is one of the most stringent in recent memory but next year's may be even tighter, state Finance Commissioner John Ferguson said Tuesday.
"We'll have the issue of dealing with choices again," Ferguson said.
The budget that took effect Tuesday eliminated 700 state jobs through cuts to state agencies.

Economic growth should bring the state about $250 million of new revenue in fiscal 1998, Ferguson said. But he anticipates several demands on the money including repayment of $110 million to reserve funds raided to balance this year's budget.
That includes $45 million drawn from Tennessee Housing and Development Agency reserves and $40 million needed for debt service on bonds that have been authorized but not yet issued.
Operating costs for a state prison under construction in Lauderdale County will add another $20 million to $22 million.
The state probably also will have to raise its funding of TennCare, the state health insurance program for the poor, by $30 million to offset a likely reduction in federal grants, Ferguson said.

Costs are expected to rise by tens of millions for Tennessee's Families First welfare-to-work program and its basic education program, due to inflation and growth in the student population, Ferguson said.
The expenses would leave little money for capital projects and salary increases for state employees, who are expected to receive a 1.5 percent pay hike in January.
The raise is contingent on an actuarial study that will determine whether the state can reduce contributions to their retirement fund.

At a meeting last week, the Tennessean reported, state Sen. Douglas Henry asked Ferguson repeatedly whether Gov. Don Sundquist's next budget would raid state reserve funds again. Ferguson declined to answer.
"That worries me," said Henry, D-Nashville. In a reference to bond rating agencies, he said, "If we keep this up, those boys up in New York will put a hard eye on us."
